title: “It’s not just about the app”: managerial responses to customer concerns in digital banking
abstract: Purpose As digital banking becomes central to financial operations, banks face persistent challenges concerning customer complaints, trust, security and uneven digital engagement. This study aims to examine how bank managers interpret and respond to these challenges, foregrounding managerial sensemaking as a critical determinant of institutional practice. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 48 bank managers in Pakistan, this study adopts an abductive application of the Gioia methodology. By mobilizing service recovery logic, trust and perceived risk theory and the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT), the research systematically connects managerial interpretations with established theoretical perspectives. Findings The analysis reveals four aggregate dimensions: accessibility, impact on profit and loss, integrated security and banking practices and digitalization. The findings demonstrate that digital banking challenges are not merely technical; they are organizational tensions managed through complex interpretive work. Specifically, this study reveals how managers reconcile the gap between institutional digital readiness, as defined by UTAUT’s facilitating conditions, and customer-level adoption barriers. Originality/value By foregrounding managerial sensemaking, this study extends service recovery and trust-based perspectives, offering new theoretical insights into how banks navigate risk, perceived fairness and customer confidence in emerging economy financial environments.

Validating CEFR writing benchmarks in Asian EFL higher education: cross-national corpus evidence for assessment quality and regional calibration
abstract: Purpose This study aims to evaluate whether a uniform Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) writing benchmark represents English as a Foreign Language writing production across 22 Asia-Pacific university contexts. Discriminant validity of CEFR labels and homogeneity of production norms across national systems are treated as testable assessment-validity questions. Design/methodology/approach Token count, indexing productive fluency, and type-token ratio (TTR), indexing lexical diversity, were computed for 29,420 essays from the International Corpus Network of Asian Learners of English across two parallel writing tasks. Welch ANOVA with Games–Howell correction was applied after rejection of the homogeneity-of-variance assumption. Findings Token count increased across CEFR levels in both tasks, while TTR increased more modestly. The smoking restriction task did not separate the two upper levels on token count, although TTR did, indicating that detection of a proficiency difference depends on the index chosen. At matched proficiency, Southeast Asian learners produced longer texts than East Asian learners, while the lexical diversity differential was small and varied across levels. Research limitations/implications Both indices capture surface production; curriculum data were unavailable. Practical implications Multitopic assessment and regional production norm profiles can inform CEFR calibration. Social implications Benchmark differences at matched proficiency carry consequences for academic mobility and university access. Originality/value Two complementary indices across 22 systems and two tasks provide a previously unavailable calibration baseline, linked to an argument-based account of assessment validity.

title: The power of inclusivity: from inclusive workplace practices to customer trust, loyalty and purchase intention
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study was to examine how lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (LGBTQ+) employee support, defined as companies' support for their LGBTQ+ employees, relates to customers' social media engagement [1], their brand association, trust, loyalty and purchase intention. Design/methodology/approach Partial Least Square-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to analyze survey data from 273 LGBTQ+ consumers and to explore the relationships between LGBTQ+ employee support and customers' brand association, social media engagement, trust, loyalty and purchase intention. Additionally, PROCESS Macro was used (Hayes, 2022) for simple and serial mediation analyses. Findings Results indicate that LGBTQ+ employee support is positively associated with customer brand associations, social media engagement and trust. Social media engagement emerged as a stronger predictor of trust than customer brand association. Furthermore, mediation analysis revealed that customers' brand association, social media engagement and trust serve as important pathways linking employee support to consumer purchase intention. Originality/value This study demonstrates how managers can prioritize LGBTQ+ employee support within their organizations to build trust among LGBTQ+ individuals, which, in turn, fosters loyalty. The findings also offer business managers an important strategic roadmap for engaging LGBTQ+ individuals in digital environments and strengthening customer brand associations. By doing so, firms can enhance trust and loyalty, ultimately improving purchase intention. Methodologically, the study departs from generic inclusivity cues by using company-specific stimuli drawn from the published Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) policies and reports of 15 firms, validated through independent expert ratings, and it combines PLS-SEM with PROCESS-based serial mediation analysis and a Gaussian copula test for endogeneity to strengthen the robustness of the inferences.

title: Co-creating public value in rural micro-municipalities: collaborative governance under proximity and capacity constraints
journal: International Journal of Public Sector Management
abstract: Purpose This study addresses a central public management problem: how structurally capacity-constrained public organisations mobilise, coordinate and sustain resources distributed across civic, private and community actors for public service provision. Using a rural micro-municipality as a revealing empirical setting, it examines how organisational capacity and relational proximity condition public value co-creation and collaborative service provision. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an in-depth qualitative case study of Gagliano Aterno, Italy. Data collected between 2023 and 2025 combine semi-structured interviews, direct observation, participatory action research, participatory mapping and sensemaking activities, enabling a processual and multi-actor analysis of collaborative governance. Findings Capacity constraints encourage the municipality to mobilise distributed resources through adaptive coordination, but also make this orchestration fragile. Public value trajectories are non-linear and may become vulnerable to erosion as successful mobilisation generates additional demands on finite civic and organisational resources, while proximity operates as an ambivalent governance condition: dense relationships facilitate trust, mobilisation and responsiveness, yet can concentrate voice, reinforce dependence on established networks and produce uneven participation. Civic resources expand operational capacity but cannot compensate indefinitely for limited organisational capacity. Originality/value The paper contributes to public management by explaining how scarce municipal capacity, orchestration demands and relational proximity interact in collaborative service provision. Capacity constraints increase reliance on distributed civic and private resources, which expands the need for orchestration; proximity facilitates this coordination while differentiating opportunities for participation and influence. The concept of fragile orchestration captures how these dynamics can extend public action while leaving coordination vulnerable where organisational resources for stabilising distributed contributions remain constrained.
